body.title: fix(runner): show the real total in the list header
body.description:
## Description

`glab runner list` and `glab runner jobs` discarded the `*gitlab.Response`
from the API call, so the header only reported the number of rows on the
current page, for example `Showing 1 job on . (Page 3)` for a runner with 10
jobs.

This keeps the response and passes `resp.TotalItems` to the list title, the
same approach as !4165 (`ci list`) and !4166 (`release list`):

- `runner list` reads, for example, `Showing 1 of 2 runners on OWNER/REPO. (Page 1)`.
  All three scopes are covered: project (default), `--group`, and `--instance`.
- `runner jobs` reads, for example, `Showing 1 of 10 jobs on . (Page 3)`.
- When the response carries no total, the header stays as it is today.

Only the header line changes. The table and `--output json` are unchanged.

`runner managers` is not changed. The `GET /runners/:id/managers` endpoint is
not paginated: it returns every manager in one response with no `X-Total`
header, so the current `Showing N managers` is already the full count. The
command has no `--page` or `--per-page` flags either.

`runner jobs` and `runner managers` print `on .` because they don't set a
scope name in the title. That predates this change, so I've left it out of
this MR. I'm happy to look at it in a follow-up if it's worth fixing.

## Related Issues

Closes #8652

Related to #1165

## How has this been tested?

- Added `TestRunnerList_HeaderTotal` in
  `internal/commands/runner/list/list_test.go`. It has one case per scope
  (project, `--group`, `--instance`) that returns `TotalItems: 11` for
  `--page 2 --per-page 5` and expects `Showing 1 of 11 runners on <scope>. (Page 2)`,
  plus a case without a total that keeps `Showing 1 runner ...`.
- Added `TestRunnerJobs_HeaderTotal` in
  `internal/commands/runner/jobs/jobs_test.go`, with a case that returns
  `TotalItems: 53` and expects `Showing 1 of 53 jobs on . (Page 3)`, and a case
  without a total.
- The new cases with a total fail without this change, and pass with it.
- `go test ./internal/commands/runner/...` passes.
- `go vet ./internal/commands/runner/...` passes.
- `golangci-lint run ./internal/commands/runner/...` (v2.14.0) reports 0
  issues, and `golangci-lint fmt --diff` reports no changes.
- `go run ./scripts/comment-overlap` reports no findings in the changed files.
- Ran a build of this branch and a build of `main` against a self-managed
  instance where I own the runners:

  | Command | `main` | This branch |
  |---|---|---|
  | `glab runner list -P 1` | `Showing 1 runner on <project>. (Page 1)` | `Showing 1 of 2 runners on <project>. (Page 1)` |
  | `glab runner list --instance -P 1 -p 2` | `Showing 1 runner on instance. (Page 2)` | `Showing 1 of 2 runners on instance. (Page 2)` |
  | `glab runner jobs <id> -P 1 -p 3` | `Showing 1 job on . (Page 3)` | `Showing 1 of 10 jobs on . (Page 3)` |
  | `glab runner managers <id>` | `Showing 1 manager on . (Page 1)` | `Showing 1 manager on . (Page 1)` |

  The table body and `-F json` output are byte-identical to `main`.

body.title: fix(df): fail closed when the policy API stops answering
body.description:
## Description

If the Dependency Firewall API accepts the connection and never answers (for example behind a stalled load balancer), a package manager under `glab df` hangs until the user presses Ctrl-C. It should fail closed after `policy.CheckTimeout` (60s), as that constant's doc comment promises.

The callers do pass a 60s deadline. `CachingChecker` then runs the shared check under `context.WithoutCancel`, so that one caller walking away doesn't cancel the check for every caller waiting on the same coordinate. `WithoutCancel` also drops the deadline, and the API client has no overall or response-header timeout, so nothing ends the call.

`CachingChecker` now puts the caller's deadline back on the shared check and still ignores the caller's cancellation. A stalled check ends at the deadline as `policy check failed: … context deadline exceeded`, which blocks the package. As with any other failure, the entry is dropped, so a later request retries it.

This affects every ecosystem that goes through the MITM proxy, and the Go module gate in !4168. It was found in review of !4168.

## How has this been tested?

- `TestCacheStalledCheckFailsClosedAtCallerDeadline`: a checker that returns only when its context ends. It hung past the 5s guard before the fix, and now returns Blocked at the 50ms deadline.
- `TestCacheCallerCancellationDoesNotEndSharedCheck` pins the existing behaviour this must keep: a cancelled caller doesn't fail the shared check. Passing the caller's context straight through would break it.
- `glab df npm install left-pad@1.3.0` against a fake GitLab API that accepts connections and never answers:

| Build | Result |
|---|---|
| `main` | still hung when `timeout` killed it at 150s |
| this branch | exit 1 after 61s: `npm error 403 … policy check failed: dependency firewall evaluation failed: context deadline exceeded` |

body.title: feat(govern): install an OpenCode plugin to sync OpenCode sessions
body.description:
## What does this MR do and why?

glab can already read OpenCode sessions with `opencode export`, but only when it runs with `OPENCODE_SESSION_ID` set. Nothing ever did that: glab installed nothing in OpenCode, and OpenCode doesn't set that variable itself (it only sets `OPENCODE=1` and `OPENCODE_PID`). So OpenCode sessions never got synced.

This adds a small plugin that `glab govern setup --agents opencode` installs in OpenCode's global plugin directory, `~/.config/opencode/plugins/glab-govern.js` (or under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`). At the end of each turn it runs `glab govern audit sync --silent` with the session ID.

- It works with OpenCode 1.4 or later and OpenCode 2. It's one default export, with `server` for 1 (which syncs on `session.idle`) and `setup` for 2. OpenCode 2 doesn't send `session.idle` or `session.status` to plugins, so on 2 it syncs on `session.execution.succeeded`, `failed` or `interrupted`.
- OpenCode 2 also moved export and changed its format. glab runs `opencode session export --standalone <id>` and falls back to `opencode export <id>`, and reads both formats. `--standalone` keeps the scheduled job from starting OpenCode's background service.
- The plugin drops `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` before running glab, so OpenCode started from inside Claude Code is still synced as OpenCode.
- glab is started detached. `opencode run` exits about half a second after the session goes idle, and an awaited sync got killed before it sent anything.
- It's only installed when you pass `--agents opencode`, so nobody gets OpenCode syncing without asking. Later setups keep it up to date. `--agents opencode` on its own leaves Codex and Cursor discovery alone.
- Choosing any agent, Claude Code included, is in a follow-up MR on top of this one.
- glab marks the file with a first line and won't overwrite or remove a file it didn't write.
- `setup --uninstall` removes it, and `doctor` has a new "OpenCode plugin" check.
- `audit sync --all` now pauses OpenCode sessions when the plugin is missing, same as Claude Code with the Stop hook. If anyone was syncing OpenCode their own way, `--all` will skip those sessions until they run `setup --agents opencode`.

Part of https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/634428. Not in this MR: the `source` label (#632997), `agent_version`, and sending prompts, responses and token counts. The export has all of these, so they can follow.

## How to set up and validate locally

I tested this end to end with OpenCode 2.1.2 and 1.19.3, using the same plugin file, in a sandboxed HOME, against https://gitlab.com/compliance-group-testing-and-demos/team-testing-subgroup/jeanvdw/ai-tracking. For 2, I found the event names and fields by logging every event it sends to a plugin. Sessions from both were created and synced through the plugin alone:

1. `make build`, then `glab govern setup --agents opencode --no-fallback-sync`. It prints `OpenCode plugin installed in ~/.config/opencode/plugins/glab-govern.js`.
1. `glab govern doctor` shows `OpenCode plugin: installed in ...`.
1. In a repo whose remote has governance on, run `opencode run "Run ls once"`.
1. The session shows up in the project as `agent_type: opencode`, with its tool events. The plugin does this on its own, no `sync --all` needed.
1. `glab govern setup --uninstall` removes only `glab-govern.js` and leaves other plugins alone. After that, `glab govern audit sync --all` says OpenCode is paused.

Things I noticed and left for follow-ups:

- Subagent sessions (the `task` tool) probably go idle too, so each one would sync as its own session. Haven't tested that yet.
- The plugin finds `glab` on OpenCode's PATH, same as the Claude Code hooks.

body.title: feat(df): add a loopback Go module proxy that gates module zips
body.description:
## Description

Adds `internal/dependencyfirewall/gomodproxy`, the enforcement point for the upcoming `glab df go`. Nothing calls it yet; the next MR wires it into the run engine.

It's a small server on `127.0.0.1` that speaks the [Go module proxy protocol](https://go.dev/ref/mod#goproxy-protocol). `glab df go` will point `go` at it with `GOPROXY`, so every module `.zip` passes through it:

- A `.zip` request is parsed into a module path and version and checked against the project's Dependency Firewall policy. A blocked zip gets a `403` with a `text/plain` reason that `go` prints, and is never fetched.
- Allowed zips, and the metadata requests (`.info`, `.mod`, `@latest`, version lists, `/sumdb/`), go to a backend built on [goproxy](https://github.com/goproxy/goproxy), which fetches them.
- Plain HTTP on loopback means no certificate is involved, which is why this replaces the closed !3928 MITM matcher for Go: `go` before 1.27 on macOS, and `git`, reject the MITM CA unless it's installed with `sudo`.

This is ported from the !3910 proof of concept, with these changes:

| Change | Why |
|---|---|
| A random per-run path token in the server URL, and a `Host` check | The backend fetches with the user's credentials. Without these, another local process, or a web page using DNS rebinding, could read private modules through it. |
| `Stop` cancels in-flight checks and drains for at most 5s, then force-closes | The PoC could make Ctrl-C wait about 65s. This matches the MITM proxy's 5s drain. A check the production `CachingChecker` won't cancel no longer delays `Stop` or records a verdict after it. |
| Only blocked and warned zips record verdicts; `CheckedZips` counts every decision | Matches the MITM proxy. The count lets the next MR say "nothing was checked" when every module came from the cache. |
| `golang.org/toolchain` is exempt only for toolchain-shaped versions | The PoC exempted any version of that path. |
| The fetcher pins `GOTOOLCHAIN=local`, `GOWORK=off` and `-modcacherw`, and those pins can't be overridden | Keeps the fetcher from downloading a toolchain, applying a workspace, or leaving an undeletable module cache. Overriding its private module cache would let `go` skip the gated request. |

The parser cuts the module path at the first `/@`, as goproxy's own router does. `@` is illegal in module paths and `/` in versions, so a second `/@v/` lands in the version, where `module.UnescapeVersion` refuses it. Every finding from the !3928 review (version unescaping, dot segments, empty module path, a second `/@v/`, malformed `!` escapes, percent escapes) has a named test.

## Dependencies

- **`github.com/goproxy/goproxy` v0.27.0.** The standard library has no Go module proxy protocol implementation, and no existing glab dependency provides one. Writing it by hand would mean reimplementing version queries, pseudo-version resolution, the `go mod download` direct path, and checksum-database proxying. goproxy is only the backend behind glab's own gate; the gate makes every policy decision. It's wired in as middleware rather than as a custom `Fetcher`, because goproxy maps every `Fetcher` error to 404 or 500, and a 404 is what makes `go` fall through to another source. v0.27.0 caps upstream `.mod`/`.zip` sizes. The build footprint is goproxy, `golang.org/x/mod` and `github.com/aofei/backoff`; goproxy's `cmd/` and S3 trees aren't imported.
- **`golang.org/x/mod` v0.42.0** (now direct). The gate decodes module paths and versions with `module.UnescapePath`/`UnescapeVersion`, exactly as `cmd/go` encodes them. It's pinned explicitly because `go get` of goproxy alone would keep an older version, and x/mod below v0.40.0 has [GO-2026-6179](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6179), a checksum-database verification bypass reachable through goproxy. goproxy v0.27.0 itself requires v0.42.0.

`govulncheck` reports no vulnerabilities for the package.

## Notes for the next MR

- Switch the `"golang"` ecosystem literal to `purl.TypeGolang` once !4167 merges. Until then the REST checker rejects `golang`, and the gate fails closed.
- Call `Server.Stop` before `Backend.Close`.
- A stalled policy API hung the gate, because `CachingChecker` dropped the `policy.CheckTimeout` deadline and the API client has no timeout of its own. The MITM proxy on `main` hangs the same way. !4178 fixes it in `CachingChecker` for both, so this MR doesn't change `check`.
- `Server.record`/`Verdicts` repeat the MITM proxy's verdict dedupe, and `cilog.Append` has a third copy. A shared `verdict.Collector` for both proxies is a follow-up after the Go MRs merge.

## How has this been tested?

- Package tests with `-race` and `goleak`. These cover the token and `Host` refusals, bounded `Stop` while a policy check or backend request hangs (including one wrapped in `CachingChecker`), the fetcher pins and overrides, the toolchain exemption, and every parser finding above. The tests for new behavior were written first and seen failing against the PoC code.
- Tests added after a second review, each seen failing against a mutant that removes its guard: an error after `Stop` is not recorded as a verdict, the `path.Clean` refusal of dot segments behind the sumdb prefix and of a trailing slash, and the sanitizer's removal of format runes such as U+200B, which make `go` drop the whole block reason. The error-after-`Stop` path is a select race, so that test runs the check 100,000 times. It caught the mutant in 50 of 50 runs and takes 0.6s under `-race`.
- A real `go mod download` against the server with a stub policy that blocks `rsc.io/sampler`: `rsc.io/quote@v1.5.2` downloaded through the tokened `GOPROXY` URL with one zip checked, and `rsc.io/sampler@v1.3.0` was refused with the firewall reason and recorded as blocked.
- Code review covered correctness, project standards, testing, maintainability, security, reliability and adversarial lenses. Its findings were applied, apart from one consistency nit about hand-stamped verdict timestamps: dropping them would change the recorded time from decision time to log-write time.

body.title: feat(df): check golang PURLs in glab df package
body.description:
## Description

`glab df package` now accepts Go modules: `pkg:golang/<module path>@<version>` is checked against the project's Dependency Firewall policy with ecosystem `golang`.

packageurl-go lowercases golang namespaces and names, as the PURL spec says, but Go module paths are case-sensitive: `github.com/BurntSushi/toml` and `github.com/burntsushi/toml` are different modules to `go`. The golang name is rebuilt from the raw PURL path, so glab sends the module path as written. The upcoming `glab df go` command sends the same case-kept path, so both commands send the same coordinate and users see the real module path.

This is the first of four MRs that add Go support through a local module proxy instead of the closed !3928 matcher:

1. This MR: golang in `purl`, the policy client and `glab df package`.
2. !4168: the `gomodproxy` package on its own.
3. !4169: the run-engine wiring, the Go manager and `glab df go`.
4. !4170: the user's own `GOPROXY` as the upstream.

This MR and !4168 don't depend on each other and can merge in either order.

## How the server matches golang names

The policy API folds case for golang, so a module can't get past a rule by changing case. `EvaluatePackageService#normalized_name` runs `Sbom::PackageUrl::Normalizer`, which lowercases `golang` names, and both the advisory lookup and the policy rules use that lowercased name.

One server-side quirk, read from the source and not exercised: `Rule#purl_excepted?` compares a policy's exception PURL to `pkg:golang/<lowercased name>` exactly, and the policy editor stores exceptions as typed. An exception written in mixed case, such as `pkg:golang/github.com/Masterminds/goutils@v1.1.0`, therefore never matches, and the module stays blocked. This fails safe and affects every client, not only glab.

## How has this been tested?

- Unit tests: golang PURL parsing (plain, mixed case, no namespace, `+incompatible` version, qualifiers and subpath ignored, a percent-encoded segment, the `pkg://` form, and `@` inside the qualifiers and subpath), the `golang` ecosystem mapping, and the evaluate request `glab df package` sends for `pkg:golang/github.com/BurntSushi/toml@v1.4.0`.
- A real `glab df package` run against GDK (`gitlab-org/df-test`, which inherits the "Deny high volume" vulnerability policy):

| PURL | Name in GDK's `api_json.log` | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `pkg:golang/github.com/Masterminds/goutils@v1.1.0` | `github.com/Masterminds/goutils` | blocked, exit 3 |
| `pkg:golang/github.com/masterminds/goutils@v1.1.0` | `github.com/masterminds/goutils` | blocked, exit 3 |
| `pkg:golang/github.com/Masterminds/goutils@v1.1.1` (fixed version) | `github.com/Masterminds/goutils` | allowed, exit 0 |
| `pkg:golang/golang.org/x/net@v0.0.0-20181017193950-04a2e542c03f` | `golang.org/x/net` | blocked, exit 3 |

- A real `glab df package` run with the fake policy checker, which matches names exactly, blocking `golang:github.com/BurntSushi/toml@v1.4.0`. This shows the path glab sends keeps its case:

| PURL | Result |
|---|---|
| `pkg:golang/github.com/BurntSushi/toml@v1.4.0` | blocked, exit 3 |
| `pkg:golang/github.com/burntsushi/toml@v1.4.0` | allowed, exit 0 |
| `pkg:golang/github.com/pkg/errors@v0.9.1` | allowed, exit 0 |

body.title: fix(release): show the real total in the list header
body.description:
## Description

`glab release list` discarded the `*gitlab.Response` from `ListReleases` inside
`listReleases`, so the header only reported the number of rows on the current
page. `gitlab-org/cli`, with 163 releases, showed
`Showing 30 releases on gitlab-org/cli.`

This returns the response from `listReleases` and passes `resp.TotalItems` to
the list title, the same approach as !4101 (`schedule list`):

- The header reads, for example, `Showing 30 of 163 releases on gitlab-org/cli.`
- When the response carries no total, the header stays as it is today.

Only the header line changes. The table and `--output json` are unchanged.

Unlike the other list commands, `release list` sets `title.Page = 0`, so its
header has no `(Page N)` suffix even with `--page`. That line predates the
`--page` and `--per-page` flags, which were added in 7340cf1e5 without updating
it. I've left it as is to keep this MR to the total, and I'm happy to fix it
here or in a follow-up.

## Related Issues

Closes #8651

Related to #1165

## How has this been tested?

- `internal/commands/release/list/release_list_test.go`:

  - Added `TestReleaseList_HeaderTotal` with a case that returns

body.title: fix(ci): show the real total in the list header
body.description:
## Description

`glab ci list` discarded the `*gitlab.Response` from `ListProjectPipelines`, so
the header only reported the number of rows on the current page. A project with
hundreds of pipelines showed `Showing 20 pipelines on OWNER/REPO. (Page 1)`.

This keeps the response and passes `resp.TotalItems` to the list title, the same
approach as !4057 (`issue list`) and !4101 (`schedule list`):

- The header reads, for example,
  `Showing 20 of 328 pipelines on OWNER/REPO. (Page 1)`. With `--status`, the
  total is the filtered count, for example `Showing 15 of 15 failed pipelines`.
- When the response carries no total, the header stays as it is today.

Only the header line changes. The table and `--output json` are unchanged.

## Related Issues

Closes #8650

Related to #1165

## How has this been tested?

- `internal/commands/ci/list/list_test.go`: added `TestCiListHeaderTotal` with
  three cases:
  - `TotalItems: 326` with `--per-page 20 --page 17` expects
    `Showing 1 of 326 pipelines on OWNER/REPO. (Page 17)`.
  - `--status failed` with `TotalItems: 61` expects
    `Showing 1 of 61 failed pipelines ...`.
  - a response without a total keeps `Showing 1 pipeline ...`.

  The first two fail without this change. The existing tests return a nil
  response and pass unchanged.
- `go test ./internal/commands/ci/...` passes, and
  `go test -race -count=3 ./internal/commands/ci/list/` passes.
- `go vet ./internal/commands/ci/list/` passes.
- `golangci-lint run ./internal/commands/ci/list/...` (v2.14.0) reports 0
  issues, and `golangci-lint fmt --diff` reports no changes.
- `go run ./scripts/comment-overlap` reports 0 findings.
- Ran a build of this branch against a self-managed GitLab 19.3.3-ee instance:

  | Command | `main` | This branch |
  |---|---|---|
  | `glab ci list` | `Showing 20 pipelines on OWNER/REPO. (Page 1)` | `Showing 20 of 328 pipelines on OWNER/REPO. (Page 1)` |
  | `glab ci list -p 2` | `Showing 20 pipelines on OWNER/REPO. (Page 2)` | `Showing 20 of 328 pipelines on OWNER/REPO. (Page 2)` |
